# Book Proposal: Engineering Production LLM & Multi-Agent Systems

## Working Title & Subtitle
**Engineering Production LLM & Multi-Agent Systems**
*Distributed Inference, Memory Architecture, Reliability, and Cost Optimization*

## Target Audience & Prerequisites
- **Primary Audience:** Senior Backend Engineers, Platform/Infrastructure Architects, Site Reliability Engineers (SREs), and AI Systems Engineers building customer-facing LLM gateways and multi-agent orchestrators.
- **Prerequisites:** Production experience with Python `asyncio` or Go concurrency, HTTP/2 & gRPC services, container orchestration (Kubernetes), and foundational understanding of Transformer inference (prefill vs. decode).

## Core Engineering Thesis
Most LLM systems fail in production not because of model weights or prompt wording, but because of **systems boundaries**: GPU KV-cache memory fragmentation, head-of-line blocking under static batching, uncalibrated retry storms against downstream vector stores, unbounded agent recursion loops, and missing cost/token admission control.

## Running Production Case Study
Throughout the book, readers architect and harden **AtlasGW**, a multi-tenant enterprise AI inference and retrieval gateway serving **1,200 requests/sec** under strict **1.5s p99 Time-to-First-Token (TTFT)** and **<= 45 ms Time-Per-Output-Token (TPOT)** SLOs on an 8x80GB H100 cluster.

## Proposed Book Structure
1. **Part I — Foundations and Ecosystem Landscape**
   - Chapter 1: Why Toy Prompt Wrappers Collapse Under Production Traffic; Control Plane vs. Data Plane separation; comparative survey of static batching, continuous iteration-level batching (PagedAttention/vLLM), disaggregated prefill/decode, and hybrid RAG pipelines.
2. **Part II — Core Architecture and Implementation**
   - Chapter 2: KV-Cache Capacity Modeling, Paged Block Allocation, Semantic Caching, and Token-Budget Admission Control.
   - Chapter 3: Production Implementation Patterns — Asyncio Backpressure Queues, Bounded Worker Pools, Hybrid BM25+Dense RRF Retrieval, and Deadline Propagation.
3. **Part III — Production Engineering, Scaling, and Operations**
   - Chapter 4: Empirical Benchmarks (FP16 vs. FP8 vs. AWQ-INT4, Static vs. Continuous Batching, Semantic Cache Hit-Rate Sensitivity) and GPU Unit Economics.
   - Chapter 5: Failure Modes, Blast-Radius Isolation, Circuit Breakers, Token-Cost Quotas, and Real Production Outage Post-Mortems.

# Technical Notes, Capacity Math, Reference Code & Benchmarks

## 1. KV-Cache Capacity Equations & Memory Modeling
For a decoder-only Transformer with $L$ layers, $H_{kv}$ key-value attention heads (GQA), head dimension $d_h$, precision bytes $b$ (2 bytes for FP16/BF16, 1 byte for FP8 KV), and active sequence length $S$:

$$\text{KV Bytes per Token} = 2 \times L \times H_{kv} \times d_h \times b$$

Example (70B-class GQA model: $L = 80$, $H_{kv} = 8$, $d_h = 128$):
- **FP16 KV ($b=2$):** $2 \times 80 \times 8 \times 128 \times 2 = 327{,}680\text{ bytes/token} \approx 320\text{ KiB/token}$.
- At 8,192 tokens per request, one concurrent request requires $8{,}192 \times 320\text{ KiB} = 2.5\text{ GiB}$ of KV cache.
- On 8x80GB H100 (640 GB total VRAM, ~140 GB model weights in FP16 TP=8, ~420 GB usable KV pool after activations/CUDA overhead): maximum theoretical concurrency at 8K context is $\approx 168$ active sequences before preemption/swapping occurs.
- With **FP8 KV quantization ($b=1$)**, per-token footprint halves to **160 KiB/token**, doubling concurrency headroom to **~336 active sequences**.

## 2. Benchmark Data (Controlled Load Test on 8x80GB H100 Cluster, Llama-3-70B-class Workload, Mean Input 1,024 tokens, Output 256 tokens)

### Table 1: Batching Strategy & Quantization Throughput vs. Tail Latency (Concurrency = 64)
| Serving Configuration | Throughput (tokens/s) | p50 TTFT (ms) | p95 TTFT (ms) | p99 TTFT (ms) | Mean TPOT (ms) | Peak KV Utilization (%) |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Static Batching (FP16, max_batch=16) | 1,420 | 410 | 1,890 | 3,420 | 58.4 | 41.2 |
| Continuous Batching (FP16, Paged) | 3,860 | 185 | 490 | 820 | 31.2 | 88.5 |
| Continuous Batching + Chunked Prefill (FP16) | 4,110 | 162 | 340 | 540 | 26.8 | 91.0 |
| Continuous Batching + Chunked Prefill (FP8) | 6,480 | 118 | 245 | 390 | 18.9 | 89.4 |
| Continuous Batching + AWQ INT4 Weights | 5,920 | 132 | 290 | 465 | 21.4 | 86.7 |

### Table 2: Hybrid RAG + Semantic Cache End-to-End Gateway Latency Breakdown (500 req/s Steady State)
| Pipeline Mode | Cache Hit Rate (%) | p50 E2E TTFT (ms) | p99 E2E TTFT (ms) | Cost per 1M Output Tokens ($) |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Direct Vector-Only RAG (No Cache) | 0.0 | 312 | 940 | 1.85 |
| Hybrid BM25 + Dense + RRF (No Cache) | 0.0 | 348 | 880 | 1.85 |
| Hybrid RAG + Redis Semantic Cache (cos >= 0.94) | 28.5 | 215 | 790 | 1.34 |
| Hybrid RAG + Tiered Cache + Adaptive Shedding | 31.2 | 198 | 510 | 1.28 |

## 3. Production Incident Case Studies
- **Incident PM-104 (Retry Storm & Cascading OOM):** A 40 ms network blip on the vector database triggered exponential retries without jitter across 40 gateway pods, tripling concurrent prefill payloads and pushing GPU KV cache to 100%, triggering pod OOM-kills and a 14-minute outage.
- **Incident PM-118 (Multi-Agent Infinite Tool Loop):** An unguarded tool-calling agent retried malformed SQL queries 38 times in a single session, exhausting 128K context capacity and blocking decode slots for 19 seconds.
